name: english_04
context: An English tweet from the SemEval-2017 sentiment analysis dataset. The tweets were found by searching Twitter for popular topics of the time, such as public figures, products, places, events and political issues, and were posted between 2012 and early 2017. At least five crowd workers labelled the overall sentiment of each tweet.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 1 was 433 words, over the 400-word limit. The approach is unchanged. Annotators judge the valence of the content, not only explicit emotion:
- Good news and promotional invitations are positive.
- Reports of bad events are negative.
- Routine plans, light chit-chat and jokey gripes about trivial things are neutral.

To get under the limit:
- The rule is shorter.
- Each label keeps three examples; the Magic Mike example is dropped from positive.
- The cue lists are shorter.
- The question is shortened to a single clause.

Version 1 scored 67.3, down from 72.7 in version 0. Neutral recall fell from 130 to 101.

Cause: telling the model to judge whether the news was good or bad, and to treat promotions as positive, pushed many neutral texts to positive and negative:
- event ads and drink specials
- 'Join us' posts
- box office and sports stats
- news about Ebola, executions and Tidal

Positive recall did not improve either. Annotators are inconsistent on news and promos, but on balance they treat neutral-toned reports and ads as neutral.

Plan: return to version 0's author-feeling framing, which scored better, and make small targeted fixes:
- Tributes, condolences and RIP messages that celebrate a person are positive. The Gifford posts were wrongly labelled negative.
- Ads, event listings, reminders, giveaways and score updates are neutral unless the author adds their own enthusiasm.
- Headlines about deaths, executions, disease or crime are negative only if they are framed as bad.
- Keep the guidance that mild jokes are neutral.
- Note that personal plans the author clearly looks forward to are positive.

Version 2 scored 70.4, version 1 scored 67.3, and version 0 scored 72.7, the best so far.

The two leaky boundaries persist:
- Positive texts labelled neutral, about 49 per run.
- Negative texts labelled neutral, about 40–44 per run.

What drives the leaks:
- Many positive-gold texts are headlines reporting clear successes: wins, records, awards, box-office #1, firsts. Version 2 kept them neutral.
- Many negative-gold texts are headlines about harm: injury, killing, violence, crashes, manslaughter charges, delays, disputes, pull-outs. Version 2 kept them neutral too.

Why version 1 failed:
- It also made plain ads and listings positive, which wrecked neutral recall. Ads and listings must stay neutral.

Plan:
- Use version 0 as the base.
- Narrow 'event valence' to news headlines only: a clear success is positive, clear harm is negative.
- Ads, reminders and event listings stay neutral unless the author themselves shows enthusiasm, for example 'Are you excited', 'Don't miss', LOVE.

The neutral-gold texts labelled negative are mostly casual gripes with humour or hyperbole: 'world is turning on itself', bruises from a ride, 'HELL NO' to a price, 'gutted'. The version 0 rule already covers these, so make it more explicit.

Version 3 scored 71.0; version 0 is still the best at 72.7.

The model over-predicts neutral: it assigned 225 neutral labels against 190 in the gold set. The largest error cells are both polar texts called neutral:
- positive labelled neutral: 49
- negative labelled neutral: 49

The positive-gold misses are mostly personal tweets with only a mild lean, which annotators still mark positive:
- I want IHOP tomorrow morning
- As long as I get Dunkin tomorrow
- off to see the Foo Fighters tomorrow
- going to Florida with the fam
- who wants to come to Madonna, I have an extra ticket
- birthday party LOL

The negative-gold misses are mild personal letdowns and subtle digs:
- dang it
- Argh
- Why oh why
- why am I sad
- I can't even play lol
- 2nd worst baseball movie
- not happy
- critical news

Promotional posts are inconsistent in the gold labels, sometimes positive and sometimes neutral. Version 1's push to make them positive hurt badly, so promos stay neutral unless the author hypes them.

The main change for version 4 is a lean rule:
- Neutral only when the tweet has no emotional lean at all.
- A personal tweet that leans pleasant (treats, trips, shows, fun plans) is positive.
- A tweet that leans unpleasant (letdowns, sighs, digs, bad outcomes) is negative.

I keep the headline-valence guidance from version 3, which helped positive recall slightly. I drop the trivial-gripes-are-neutral rule, because it pushed subtle negatives to neutral. Instead, neutral is limited to purely informational, dry or jokey-without-complaint tweets.

versions.analysis_for_next:
The previous draft was 403 words, just over the 400-word limit. The approach is unchanged: a middle ground between versions 0 and 4.
- Positive or negative only when the feeling is clear.
- Matter-of-fact plans, banter, jokes, opinions, and headlines with plain framing stay neutral.
- Explicit wanting is positive.
- Real personal letdowns and news of clear harm are negative.

To cut words, I shortened the rule and dropped the Magic Mike example from positive.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 5 scored 66.2. Its 'only when clear' threshold pushed neutral predictions to 328, against 190 in the gold set, so positive and negative recall collapsed.

Neutral predictions across versions show how sensitive the model is to this one threshold:

| Version | Neutral predictions | Macro-F1 |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 213 | 72.7 |
| 3 | 225 | 71.0 |
| 4 | 119 | 71.8 |
| 5 | 328 | 66.2 |

The target is about 180–200 neutral predictions.

Plan: keep version 4's lean framing, which gave strong polar recall, and soften it slightly:
- Require a noticeable lean, not 'even mild'.
- Make specific types neutral:
  - matter-of-fact activity reports ('leaving tomorrow', 'might watch X tonight', 'sat listening to...');
  - 'who's going with me?' questions without excitement words;
  - playful teasing or banter where the author isn't really upset;
  - news on serious topics with no stated outcome.

The polar guidance stays:
- Personal wanting, anticipation and enjoyment are positive.
- Personal letdowns and critical digs are negative.
- Clear success and clear harm in news keep their labels.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Same plan as before, trimmed to fit under 400 words. Version 6 (74.2) stays the base. The edits are small:
- Neutral now covers armchair opinions and mock-dramatic overreactions to trivial things.
- Neutral gains the Frank Ocean album example.
- Positive news explicitly includes team wins.

To save words, I dropped the Foo Fighters example from positive and shortened the cue lists.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 7 scored 73.8, against 74.2 for version 6.

What happened:
- Adding armchair opinions and mock-dramatic overreactions to neutral cut neutral→negative errors only from 39 to 30.
- It raised negative→neutral errors from 22 to 40, because annotators often do label critical opinions and digs as negative.
- The neutral-gold texts it was aimed at are inconsistent with similar negative-gold texts, so the trade is a loss.

Version 8 therefore reverts to version 6's wording, which has the best balance of polar recall and neutral recall. One small change is kept: the positive news cues now include 'beats' and 'wins'. Those were harmless and help clear success headlines.

I am not reintroducing positive-for-promos. The gold labels for promos are split roughly evenly between positive and neutral, and version 1 showed that the change damages neutral recall.

versions.analysis_for_next: The earlier draft was 403 words. It was version 8 plus one small addition to negative not_for. To fit the 400-word limit I trimmed the cue lists slightly and kept that addition: mixed tweets whose main point is excitement go to positive. The rule, examples and balance are unchanged from version 8, which scored 74.3 and is the best so far.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 9 scored 74.2, essentially the same as version 8 (74.3) and version 6 (74.2). These three versions share the same lean-based rule. The small edits between them (cue trims, one not_for clause) only move errors around within noise.

The remaining errors are mostly cases where the annotators themselves are inconsistent:
- Promos are labelled positive about as often as neutral.
- Casual plans with emoji go either way.
- Joking gripes and armchair sports opinions are split between negative and neutral.

Every larger intervention on these boundaries made things worse:
- Version 1 (promos and event valence) fell to 67.3.
- Version 5 (strict 'clear feeling' threshold) fell to 66.2.
- Version 7 (mock-dramatic gripes as neutral) fell to 73.8.

For the final version I submit version 8's exact wording. It is the best-scoring version, with near-gold label proportions (211/177/212 predicted against 209/190/201 gold), and it is under the word limit.
